https://euobserver.com/228897/in-an-over.text: First published in Deník N. Americans laugh at Europeans for not having air conditioning in their buildings. Europeans tell Americans that they would not need it if the overuse of air conditioning in the United States were not contributing to global warming. Both sides are a little bit right, but not by much. Everyday life in the US differs from Europe in many respects: more cars, wider motorways, almost no public transport, greater social inequality, larger portions in restaurants. And above all, vast space, plenty of room everywhere, horizontal expansion. Despite all these differences, my most striking recurring experience was how easy it is to catch a chill in America in summer. You land, say, in Houston, where daytime temperatures throughout the summer range between thirty and forty degrees , so roughly as it was in Europe several times already this summer, except with higher humidity, which makes the local heat more oppressive. Within two minutes, your shirt is soaked through. Then, in that damp shirt, you walk into the lobby of a hotel, a shopping mall, an office or any other building, first breathing a sigh of relief… but after a while you realise it is not such a blessing after all. Air conditioning is commonly set to 18 °C, sometimes even lower. Local people are used to such abrupt temperature changes – among other reasons because they spend as little time as possible outside buildings and vehicles. I have forgotten this lesson several times, and for each such lapse I have one American sweatshirt at home that I had to buy there on the spot. One of them even has Superman on it, because that was the only one on sale. Read more As Europe swelters, Paris judges say consumers aren’t to blame — TotalEnergies is I have never understood the American urge to cool things down ad absurdum, but it probably has something to do with those big portions, big cars and the general conviction that bigger is better. In the United States, air conditioning units (air condition, or A/C – Americans regard the European words die Klimaanlage , la clim , klimatizace with suspicion; they hear in them klima , climate , that is, politics) have been part of the standard of living since the middle of the last century. They are as common as fridges or televisions, which means that even the poorest households have them. Most Americans have never experienced life without air conditioning – unless they go on a trip to Europe. This generous approach to cooling comes at a price. Air conditioning accounts for about 20 percent of the electricity consumption of US households , on average over the whole year and the whole country. In summer it probably approaches 40 percent, and during the afternoon peak in the southern United States it is even higher. For office buildings, the figure is similar if we add together the consumption of air conditioning and ventilation. There are therefore days when a quarter to a third of the United States’ instantaneous energy production goes to running air conditioning. Cool air in intensive care Last summer I spent a few days in a large Prague hospital. I received good care there and had a bed under a window facing west. In those days it was around thirty degrees outside in the afternoon, and similar inside. The staff, tormented by the heat just like the patients, accepted it with resignation: in summer it is hot, what can you do. Then I somewhat unexpectedly ended up in intensive care (no, the heat was not to blame), which is of course not pleasant, but it did have one advantage: there was air conditioning. Being hooked up to tubes is a nuisance, and a bearable temperature cannot make up for it, but it does at least improve the situation a little. I do not know whether there is a single hospital in the Czech Republic that is fully air-conditioned; I have never been in one. I also do not know whether there is a fully air-conditioned school, library or research institution anywhere. I know air-conditioned office buildings, I know several air-conditioned modern factories, which is more for the sake of machines and products than people, and I know a number of air-conditioned cafés and restaurants, because it is good for their business. Many people have air conditioning in their cars, hardly anyone at home. To read this story, log in or subscribe Enjoy access to all articles and 25 years of archives, comment and gift articles. https://www.christiandaily.com/news/bela.text: Sergiy Melyanets. Svaboda.org (RFE/RL)/ Forum 18 Authorities in Belarus have refused to answer questions by rights group Forum 18 about two Christian religious freedom advocates sought for extradition to face unspecified criminal charges. Russian independent news outlet Sota published entries from Russia’s Federal Wanted List online earlier this month, exposing Belarusian criminal cases – without stating the charges – against Protestant preacher Sergiy Melyanets and Orthodox theologian Natallia Vasilevich, co-founder of rights group Christian Vision. Both advocates appeared on Russia’s Federal Wanted List at the request of Belarusian authorities, according to Forum 18. Neither activist received official notification of the criminal charges against them. Forum 18 on Aug. 14 called contact numbers listed on the wanted list records, but unidentified officials refused to detail the charges or confirm whether investigators were actively handling the cases. “Investigators refused to explain what criminal charges they face, why, and whether they are suspects or have had charges formally laid against them,” Forum 18 stated regarding its attempts to contact Belarusian authorities. Sergei Gerasimenya, deputy plenipotentiary for religious and ethnic affairs, declined to answer questions from Forum 18. Melyanets, a Minsk native, fled Belarus in 2024 after Minsk City Court police arrested him on March 19 of that year. Officers detained Melyanets when he attended court to offer prayerful support to journalist Igor Korney. Authorities charged Korney with “participating in an extremist formation” under Article 361-1 of the Belarusian Criminal Code for his affiliation with the banned Belarusian Association of Journalists. “I went to court to support and pray for my brother in Christ, Igor,” Melyanets told human rights organization Viasna on April 24, 2024, after escaping Belarus. “I was worried about him. Although we didn’t know each other well, we had only met a couple of times, I knew he was a Catholic and that he was going through a hard time. I knew he was alone, and I wanted my presence to somehow cheer him up. I also wanted to find out what he was being accused of and tell his family about it.” The same court sentenced Melyanets to 13 days of administrative detention, followed by an additional 12 days. Upon his release, he fled to Poland with his family. Melyanets routinely supported opposition activists by attending court hearings and praying for them. “After 2020, I asked myself: how can I help people who are in prison?” Melyanets told Christian Vision in an interview following his flight. “I could write letters; I wrote. I could deliver things; I delivered. But I also realized that I could do more. I started visiting courts so that people who were there because of repression could feel supported, see that people were praying for them, and know that others remembered them.” Melyanets actively supported Minsk’s New Life Gospel Church when authorities forcibly evicted the congregation on Feb. 17, 2021. Bailiffs used an angle grinder to cut the door lock while 30 bailiffs, police officers, and Housing Repairs and Utilities Association officials executed the eviction. “I am indignant,” Melyanets told Forum 18 at the time. “This is a hostile takeover of church property under the excuse of official papers.” Melyanets prayed outside the Minsk District Police Detention Center in August 2023 alongside New Life Church’s pastor, the Rev. Vyacheslav Goncharenko, whom authorities held at the facility. Melyanets stated that police initiated a case against him in January when officers interrogated his parents about his whereabouts and alleged connections to “extremist groups.” “Questions focused mostly on me and my activities,” Melyanets said. “They want my family and me to live in fear. But I continue to do what my Christian conscience leads me to do.” If authorities capture Melyanets or Vasilevich – or if either advocate enters countries friendly to Belarus, such as Kazakhstan, Russia, Tajikistan or Uzbekistan – they face immediate arrest and extradition to Belarus while investigators conclude their cases. Vasilevich moderates Christian Vision, an organization founded in 2020 to document violations of religious freedom. The KGB secret police later designated the group as “extremist.” Vasilevich fled Belarus in 2020. Vitebsk Regional Police requested that Russian authorities add Vasilevich to Russia’s Federal Wanted List on April 13, following a criminal case launched by Belarusian police earlier that month. On March 27, the Russian Justice Ministry had designated the Christians Against War project, founded by Christian Vision members, as a “foreign agent.” Vasilevich confirmed to Forum 18 that she received no official notification of charges or suspect status connected to the anti-war project. “In principle, it’s not surprising,” Vasilevich posted to her Telegram channel on Aug. 13. “It was expected, and it doesn’t even really stir up any emotions.” The Belarusian Interior Ministry formally added Christian Vision to its list of “extremist” organizations on April 8, 2025. On April 1, 2025, KGB secret police declared Christian Vision, its website, its social media channels, and key figures – including Vasilevich, group member Natallia Harkovich and co-founder Dzmitry Korneyenko – as “extremist.” Orsha District Police raided the homes of three relatives of Korneyenko during the same month, taking DNA samples from two family members to assist in their search. Vitebsk Regional Police placed Korneyenko on a wanted list for “supporting extremist activity” in July 2024.
